front: Which features does Windows Pro have that Home lacks?
back: BitLocker drive encryption, acting as a Remote Desktop host, joining an Active Directory domain, and Group Policy management. Home can be an RDP client but not a host.

front: NTFS vs FAT32 vs exFAT?
back: NTFS: Windows default — permissions, encryption, journaling, huge files. FAT32: universal compatibility but 4 GB max file size. exFAT: FAT32's compatibility without the 4 GB limit — the choice for large flash drives used across OSes.

front: What does UAC do?
back: User Account Control prompts for consent (or admin credentials) before actions that change system state, so malware can't silently elevate — even when the user is an administrator.

front: Name the key built-in Windows management consoles and their jobs.
back: Device Manager (drivers/hardware), Disk Management (partitions/volumes), Event Viewer (system and app logs), Task Manager (processes, startup, performance), Services (background services), Task Scheduler (automated jobs).

front: What is the Windows Registry and which tool edits it?
back: The hierarchical database of OS and application settings (hives like HKLM, HKCU). Edited with regedit — export a backup of a key before changing it.

front: Basic Linux file commands: ls, cp, mv, rm, chmod?
back: ls lists directory contents, cp copies, mv moves/renames, rm deletes, chmod changes permissions (e.g. chmod 644 file). sudo runs a command with elevated privileges.

front: What are Time Machine and Keychain on macOS?
back: Time Machine is the built-in incremental backup to an external/network disk. Keychain is the system credential store for passwords and certificates.

front: FileVault, Gatekeeper, and Force Quit — what does each do on macOS?
back: FileVault: full-disk encryption (macOS's BitLocker). Gatekeeper: blocks apps from unidentified developers from launching by default. Force Quit (⌘⌥Esc): kills a frozen app, macOS's End Task.

front: How does a mobile OS get "installed" or updated, compared to a PC?
back: No separate clean/in-place choice — routine updates are OTA (over-the-air), applied without wiping the device. A factory reset/wipe is the mobile equivalent of a clean install, used to fix a broken device or before resale, not for routine updates.

front: When would you use a Windows 'in-place upgrade' vs a clean install?
back: In-place upgrade keeps apps, settings, and files (run setup from within Windows) — least disruption. Clean install wipes the disk — for corrupted systems, hardware handoffs, or edition/architecture changes.

front: Name the common malware types.
back: Virus (attaches to files), worm (self-spreads over networks), trojan (disguised as legit software), ransomware (encrypts data for payment), spyware/keylogger (steals input and data), rootkit (hides deep with admin rights), cryptominer (steals compute).

front: Phishing vs spear phishing vs whaling vs vishing/smishing?
back: Phishing: mass fraudulent email. Spear phishing: targeted at a specific person/org. Whaling: targets executives. Vishing: by phone call. Smishing: by SMS.

front: What is multifactor authentication (MFA)?
back: Authentication using two or more different factor types: something you know (password), have (phone/authenticator/token), or are (biometric). Two passwords are not MFA — same factor type.

front: Principle of least privilege?
back: Every account gets only the access required for its job, nothing more. Users run as standard users; admin rights are separate accounts used only when needed. Limits the blast radius of compromise.

front: Rank wireless security protocols weakest to strongest.
back: WEP (broken, never use) → WPA/TKIP (deprecated) → WPA2/AES-CCMP (still common, fine) → WPA3/SAE (current best — resists offline dictionary attacks).

front: BitLocker vs EFS?
back: BitLocker encrypts the entire volume (keys usually sealed in the TPM) — protects a lost/stolen machine. EFS encrypts individual files/folders per user. BitLocker is the default answer for laptop theft scenarios.

front: Tailgating, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving — and the defenses?
back: Tailgating: following someone through a secure door → mantraps, badge-per-person policy. Shoulder surfing: watching a screen/keypad → privacy filters, awareness. Dumpster diving: recovering discarded info → shredding.

front: Key mobile device security controls?
back: Screen lock (PIN/biometric), full-device encryption, remote wipe via MDM, OS updates, app-store-only installs, and locator services. For BYOD: MDM profiles separate work data.

front: List the 7 steps of the CompTIA malware removal procedure.
back: 1) Investigate and verify malware symptoms. 2) Quarantine infected systems. 3) Disable System Restore in Windows. 4) Remediate: update anti-malware, scan and remove. 5) Schedule scans and run updates. 6) Enable System Restore and create a restore point. 7) Educate the end user.

front: What is Safe Mode and when do you use it?
back: Windows boots with minimal drivers and services (via WinRE → Startup Settings). Use it when a driver, service, or malware prevents normal boot or removal — the offending component usually isn't loaded there.

front: A BSOD appears right after a driver update. Fix?
back: Boot Safe Mode → Device Manager → Roll Back Driver. If unbootable, use WinRE (System Restore to the pre-update point, or Startup Repair). The stop code and faulting module name the culprit.

front: Browser homepage changed, constant redirects and pop-ups. Diagnosis?
back: Browser hijacker / adware. Follow the malware removal steps; also reset browser settings, remove rogue extensions and proxy settings, and check the hosts file.

front: Windows is sluggish at startup. What do you check?
back: Task Manager → Startup tab (disable heavy autoruns), background processes hogging CPU/RAM/disk, malware scan, free disk space, pending updates. On HDDs, consider an SSD upgrade.

front: Which tool shows why an application crashed?
back: Event Viewer → Windows Logs → Application: look for Error events from the app or 'Application Error'/.NET entries at the crash time, which include the faulting module.

front: What is WinRE and how do you reach it?
back: The Windows Recovery Environment: Startup Repair, System Restore, command prompt, reset, and Startup Settings (Safe Mode). Reach it via Settings → Recovery → Advanced startup, Shift+Restart, or automatically after failed boots.

front: Mobile device: apps crash and the OS is unstable after an update. First steps?
back: Restart the device, update the apps, clear the misbehaving app's cache/data, check free storage. Escalate to backing up and factory-resetting only after the simple steps fail.

front: What belongs in a good ticket?
back: User and device info, clear problem description in the user's words, steps already tried, severity/impact, and ongoing progress notes — so the next tech can pick it up cold.

front: What is chain of custody?
back: The documented, unbroken record of who collected, handled, and stored evidence and when. Required for prohibited-content incidents so evidence stands up to scrutiny — document, secure, and hand off formally.

front: ESD precautions when working inside a PC?
back: Anti-static wrist strap connected to the chassis, anti-static mat/bags for components, touch bare metal before handling parts, unplug power, don't work on carpet. Never open a PSU or CRT — capacitors hold lethal charge.

front: Full vs incremental vs differential backup?
back: Full: everything, every time. Incremental: only changes since the last backup of any kind — smallest/fastest, longest restore chain. Differential: changes since the last full — restore needs just full + latest differential.

front: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
back: 3 copies of the data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy off-site. Test restores — an unverified backup is a hope, not a backup.

front: Core elements of change management?
back: Documented request and purpose, scope, risk analysis, approval, scheduled window, rollback plan, end-user notification, and post-change documentation.

front: What is an SDS?
back: Safety Data Sheet — documents a chemical product's hazards, safe handling, first aid, and disposal (e.g., for cleaning solvents, toner). Consult it for any spill or exposure.

front: Professional communication basics with a frustrated user?
back: Listen without interrupting, stay calm and avoid being defensive, don't use jargon, set honest expectations for the fix and timeline, follow up. Never argue or minimize the problem.

front: Fileless malware vs. boot sector virus vs. stalkerware — what distinguishes each?
back: Fileless malware runs entirely in memory via legitimate tools like PowerShell, no file written. A boot sector virus infects the disk boot sector, loading before the OS. Stalkerware is covertly installed by someone with physical access to track a specific person.

front: What is RSR (Rapid Security Response)?
back: Apple's mechanism for pushing critical, small security fixes to iOS/macOS between full OS version releases, applied automatically without waiting on the next major update.

front: SAML vs. IAM vs. PAM vs. JIT access — how do they relate?
back: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the overall discipline of managing identities and their access. SAML is a protocol for federated single sign-on. PAM (Privileged Access Management) controls elevated accounts specifically, and JIT (just-in-time) access is a PAM technique granting elevated rights only for a limited task window.

front: List the common MFA factor delivery methods and their factor category.
back: Something you have: hardware token, authenticator app (TOTP), SMS code, voice call, email code. Something you are: biometrics. Something you know: password/PIN. SMS and email are weaker due to interception/account-takeover risk.

front: Script file types and their platform: .bat, .ps1, .vbs, .sh, .js, .py?
back: .bat — Windows command-line batch. .ps1 — Windows PowerShell (objects/cmdlets). .vbs — legacy Windows VBScript. .sh — macOS/Linux shell. .js — JavaScript, cross-platform (Node or browser). .py — Python, cross-platform.

front: Remote access tools — RDP, VNC, SSH, RMM, SPICE, WinRM — pick the right one for the job?
back: RDP/VNC — interactive remote desktop for a person. SSH — remote command-line/shell. RMM — centralized, at-scale management of many endpoints. SPICE — VM console access with USB/multimedia redirection. WinRM — native Windows remote command/PowerShell management.

front: Key limitations to plan around before deploying an AI tool at work?
back: Hallucinations (confident but wrong output — needs human review), bias inherited from training data, accuracy not guaranteed, and data privacy (public tools may retain submitted data) — plus policy concerns like plagiarism if AI output is passed off as original work.
